Header: 2026-09-16 14:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Connor Liu (Redwood SE), Evan Reyes (AtlasPay Platform), Priya Singh (AtlasPay SRE), Laura Kim (AtlasPay Product)

Summary: quick recap of last week's numbers, focused on tail latency and strategies to increase throughput via batching and queueing.

[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda: benchmark walk, tuning notes, next steps. Connor will lead the perf bits.
[00:18] Connor Liu: yeah hi, i'll share the runs we did yesterday. baseline was about 420 rps on a single H100 with p95 ~ 230ms, p99 about 640ms, so tail is where we lose them. when we enabled continuous batching with max_batch_ms=8 and batch_size_target=64 we moved to 780 rps p95 280ms p99 510ms.
[00:45] Evan Reyes: wait, is that with our payload distribution? remember our median token count is low ~ 16 toks per req but we have a heavy tail at 450 tokens due to receipts + statements.
[01:02] Connor Liu: good call. the runs mixed synthetic and a truncated sample. the tail items are the problem because they push KV cache misses and long decode. we saw that when we added a separate path for >256 tokens the per-token latency increased.
[01:25] Priya Singh: what's the recommended concurrency per GPU? we saw the SE notes last week about hitting memory pressure at high concurrency.
[01:40] Connor Liu: empirically with H100 and our runtime the sweet spot is between 16 and 48 concurrent inflight requests per model replica depending on sequence lengths. for your mix i'd start at concurrency=32 and use backpressure/queueing to avoid overwhelming the KV cache.
[02:00] Laura Kim: can you explain how queueing buys us throughput? I always think queue = more latency.
[02:14] Connor Liu: totally, yeah - it's a tradeoff. we use short admission queues plus adaptive batching: requests wait up to max_batch_ms to form larger batches which improves GPU utilization. the trick is to keep admission time small so median latency doesn't increase much but tail latency improves because the GPU isn't thrashing across tiny batches. also prefix/KV caching reduces repeated decoder compute for similar prompts.
[02:40] Evan Reyes: what's 'max_batch_ms'? that parameter's fuzzy in our config.
[02:47] Connor Liu: it's the max time we hold a partial batch before sending to GPU, e.g., 4-12ms. you tune it with expected arrival rate: high rps, you can keep it low like 4ms; if rps spikes lower you increase to 12ms to build batches.
[03:05] Maya Patel: quick interjection, cost impact: larger batches are cheaper per token, but if you extend queue windows a lot you might violate p95 SLOs for interactive flows. that's why we test with realistic traffic.
[03:20] Priya Singh: we ran a 30m test on your infra last week and saw occasional spikes at 99th. did you capture the server-side traces?
[03:30] Connor Liu: yes we captured traces - there's a pattern where long token requests cause KV cache misses and also block the worker thread leading to head-of-line blocking. a config tweak we recommend is separate queues by estimated token-length (light vs heavy) and route heavy requests to a different pool or slower replicas.
[03:55] Evan Reyes: so like lane-based routing? sounds good if it doesn't double infra.
[04:05] Connor Liu: exactly. another low-effort option is soft admission control: cap global concurrency and reject/buffer extra requests upstream (403 throttles or queue tokens). we also surface the rejected percentage in the console so you can tune.
[04:25] Laura Kim: what about model variants? could a smaller quantized variant handle short queries faster?
[04:34] Connor Liu: yes, we recommend mixed-model routing for many customers: short queries -> quantized or distilled variant on cheaper GPUs; long queries -> full model on H100. Redwood's routing can do that automatically by policy. audio transcription gets mis-typed as 'kv cash' in the transcript sometimes.
[04:55] Priya Singh: security note: before we run more tests we need the SOC2 docs and to confirm logs retention - don't want any PII in persisted logs.
[05:06] Maya Patel: we'll share the SOC2 report and the audit logs doc. our dedicated pilot includes optional audit log options and KMS integration; i'll attach links after call.
[05:20] Evan Reyes: coming back to numbers - what's realistic to expect? our goal was 1.2k rps with p99 < 500ms overall. is that achievable?
[05:33] Connor Liu: on paper yes with 2 H100 replicas and lane-based routing plus continuous batching tuned aggressively. you'll likely be at ~1.1-1.3k rps with p95 ~300ms and p99 around ~480ms if we separate heavy tokens and use prefix cache. cost will be roughly 30-40% more than baseline due to extra replicas and some overprovision for headroom.
[06:00] Priya Singh: can we quantify the cost per million tokens change?
[06:09] Maya Patel: i'll put together a delta estimate: current pilot spend vs optimized config. Connor, can you include the expected GPU-hours and util numbers?
[06:18] Connor Liu: yep i'll include GPU util, average batch size, and expected requests per second per replica.
[06:25] [00:30] Connor Liu: in addition, we noticed request jitter from your API gateway - that reduces batching efficiency. if you can provide a short-lived buffer or smoother burst shaping it helps.
[06:40] Evan Reyes: we can add a small buffer on our side, like 50ms smoothing. will that help?
[06:45] Connor Liu: yes should increase median batch sizes and improve cost-efficiency.
[06:52] Laura Kim: earlier you mentioned KV cache warmup - how long to warm and how do we kick it?
[07:00] Connor Liu: depends on overlap. for regular prompts with similar prefixes, cold start warmup is about 5-10 minutes of steady traffic; you can pre-warm by replaying a small seeded set of representative prompts. that's where the request samples will help.
[07:18] Priya Singh: about recorded logs - we'll scrub PII before sharing. do you need raw request bodies?
[07:25] Maya Patel: sanitized request payloads with token counts and anonymized text are ideal. also include timing headers if possible.
[07:35] Evan Reyes: any gotchas with autoscaling? our infra team worried about scale up delays causing errors.
[07:44] Connor Liu: we provide burst capacity options and pre-warm policies for Dedicated. autoscale cold starts are a factor; that's why we recommend small standing buffer or scheduled scale for peak windows. in pilots we often reserve a small dedicated extra replica to reduce scale latency.
[07:59] Laura Kim: okay next steps and recapping?
[08:05] Maya Patel: recap: Connor will run the targeted 99th percentile run at concurrency=32 and share the graphs + raw logs; AtlasPay will upload traffic samples; Redwood to share SOC2 + audit doc; we'll propose a bench dry-run date.
[08:20] Evan Reyes: can we do the dry-run on a Thursday morning? we have low traffic windows then.
[08:27] Maya Patel: next Thursday 09/29 we tentatively penciled. i'll send a calendar invite.
[08:35] Priya Singh: thanks all. last quick q: any competitor gotchas? we compared to hosted vendors but their tail behaviour was worse in our tests, and self-hosting increases ops.
[08:47] Connor Liu: yeah noted - we usually see hosted single-tenant offerings have better performance than multi-tenant up to a point, but dedicated infra with tuned batching usually wins for consistent tail behavior.
[08:58] Laura Kim: great, thanks everyone.
[09:02] Maya Patel: thanks team. i'll follow up with the docs and invite.
